qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Explain how increased orders can raise earnings for repair workers when qualified applicants are scarce and training takes time.
items.canonical_answer: Orders increase demand for repair output, so employers seek more suitably qualified workers. Supply cannot expand quickly; competing to attract or retain scarce workers can raise their earnings.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the supplied demand, supply or productivity change. Mechanism (2): develop two connected causal steps using the stated conditions. Consequence (1): link the mechanism to earnings without a guaranteed universal result.
objective_titles: Identify and analyse the factors determining earnings

items.prompt: Explain why equal hourly pay of N$25 can produce different monthly earnings for workers with 160 and 80 paid hours.
items.canonical_answer: Paid hours differ: 160 hours give N$4,000 and 80 give N$2,000. The earnings difference comes from time worked rather than the hourly rate.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Identify and analyse the factors determining earnings

items.prompt: Explain the error in calling a bookkeeper’s move to bookkeeping work in another town an increase in occupational mobility.
items.canonical_answer: The move is geographical mobility because the place changes; it does not show occupational mobility because the type of work remains bookkeeping.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): geographical movement is mistaken for a change of occupation. Boundary/test (1): same work in another place distinguishes the concepts.
objective_titles: Identify and analyse the factors determining earnings

items.prompt: Explain the difference between an occupational earnings comparison and a sector earnings comparison.
items.canonical_answer: An occupational comparison groups people by type of work; a sector comparison groups economic activities and can contain different occupations. Sector averages may therefore reflect job composition.
marking_guidance: Difference (1): type of work versus activity sector. Contrast/test (1): one occupation can occur in different sectors.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the differences in earnings between different occupational groups and different economic sectors (male/female; skilled/unskilled; private/public; agricultural/manufacturing/ services)

items.prompt: Explain why invented average monthly pay of N$6,000 for specialists and N$4,000 for assistants does not show that every specialist earns more than every assistant.
items.canonical_answer: The figures summarise groups. Individuals can lie above or below their own group average, so the two distributions may overlap.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the differences in earnings between different occupational groups and different economic sectors (male/female; skilled/unskilled; private/public; agricultural/manufacturing/ services)

items.prompt: Explain the weekly earnings difference at an invented workshop where women average 30 paid hours and men 40, with both groups paid N$30 per hour for the same task.
items.canonical_answer: The starting difference is paid hours. Equal hourly rates give women N$900 and men N$1,200 on these averages; ten additional paid hours account for the N$300 weekly gap. The data do not establish why the hours differ.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the supplied demand, supply or productivity change. Mechanism (2): develop two connected causal steps using the stated conditions. Consequence (1): link the mechanism to earnings without a guaranteed universal result.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving male and female earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain the supported conclusion when an invented employer states that equally qualified women and men doing the same work for the same hours receive different rates solely because of sex.
items.canonical_answer: The supplied cause is discriminatory pay: equivalent work and hours receive different rates because of sex. The difference cannot be explained by hours in this case.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving male and female earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain why scarce trained pump repair workers may earn more than packing assistants when both work equal hours, repair demand is strong and many packing applicants are available.
items.canonical_answer: Strong repair demand creates employer demand for the relevant skill. Suitable repair workers are scarce and hard to replace, encouraging competitive offers. More readily supplied packing labour faces less scarcity pressure, supporting a pay difference under these conditions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the supplied demand, supply or productivity change. Mechanism (2): develop two connected causal steps using the stated conditions. Consequence (1): link the mechanism to earnings without a guaranteed universal result.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving skilled and unskilled earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain why a qualification alone does not guarantee high pay when employers no longer demand the skill it certifies.
items.canonical_answer: The qualification does not create demand for the work. With weak demand for that skill, employers may offer little even if training took a long time.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving skilled and unskilled earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain a supplied private clinic’s N$12,000 monthly offer compared with N$10,000 for a similar public post: hours match, technicians are scarce and the public post has a fixed stated pay budget.
items.canonical_answer: Scarcity encourages the clinic to offer more to recruit the technician. Its funding permits N$12,000, while the public post’s stated budget constrains its offer to N$10,000. The N$2,000 gap reflects these conditions rather than an ownership rule.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the supplied demand, supply or productivity change. Mechanism (2): develop two connected causal steps using the stated conditions. Consequence (1): link the mechanism to earnings without a guaranteed universal result.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving private and public sector earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain why higher average private sector earnings do not by themselves prove a higher private wage for the same job.
items.canonical_answer: The private sector may contain a different mix of occupations. Without matching jobs and hours, the average gap does not isolate the reward for comparable work.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving private and public sector earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain the annual earnings comparison using invented figures: agricultural work pays N$4,000 monthly for six paid months; manufacturing work pays N$3,000 monthly for twelve paid months, with no other earnings included.
items.canonical_answer: Seasonal agricultural work provides fewer paid months. Its annual earnings are N$24,000 against manufacturing earnings of N$36,000. The shorter paid period more than offsets the higher monthly agricultural payment; it does not show a lower monthly rate.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the supplied demand, supply or productivity change. Mechanism (2): develop two connected causal steps using the stated conditions. Consequence (1): link the mechanism to earnings without a guaranteed universal result.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving agricultural earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain why a scarce irrigation technician can earn more than a readily supplied general farm worker when the farm needs both roles and hours are equal.
items.canonical_answer: Demand for the technician’s required skill meets a limited suitable supply. Difficulty recruiting substitutes can support a higher rate than for the more readily supplied role.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving agricultural earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain how a furniture machine raising usable output per trained operator-hour from four to six panels could support higher operator pay when extra output has buyers and trained operators are scarce.
items.canonical_answer: Equipment complements trained labour and increases its productive contribution. Orders support demand for the extra panels, while scarce operators are difficult to replace. Employers may offer more to retain them, although bargaining and funding affect the actual increase.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the supplied demand, supply or productivity change. Mechanism (2): develop two connected causal steps using the stated conditions. Consequence (1): link the mechanism to earnings without a guaranteed universal result.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving manufacturing earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain why a higher manufacturing earnings average can occur after more specialists are hired even if each existing worker’s rate stays unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Specialists can have higher pay than the previous group average. Increasing their share raises the average through workforce composition without an individual rate increase.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving manufacturing earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain why a scarce specialist repair worker may earn more than a general receptionist in an invented service business with strong specialist demand and many suitable reception applicants.
items.canonical_answer: Demand for specialist repair creates demand for its rare skill. Limited substitutes increase recruitment pressure and can support higher specialist pay; plentiful reception applicants reduce the corresponding scarcity pressure for that role.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the supplied demand, supply or productivity change. Mechanism (2): develop two connected causal steps using the stated conditions. Consequence (1): link the mechanism to earnings without a guaranteed universal result.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving service-sector earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain why expanding demand for a service need not cause a large wage rise if many suitably skilled workers can enter quickly.
items.canonical_answer: Additional labour supply can meet the stronger employer demand. Employment may expand with limited upward pressure on the wage rate because recruitment is not strongly constrained.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Explain earnings differences involving service-sector earnings; name the comparison group and explain a productivity, skill, bargaining or labour-demand cause.

items.prompt: Explain a widening pay gap when technical workers’ productivity and demand rise, their skill remains scarce, but assistants face unchanged demand and many applicants.
items.canonical_answer: Technical productivity and demand strengthen employers’ willingness to recruit or retain technical workers. Restricted skill supply increases competitive pay pressure. Assistants lack the same demand and scarcity changes, so technical earnings can grow faster and widen the gap.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the supplied demand, supply or productivity change. Mechanism (2): develop two connected causal steps using the stated conditions. Consequence (1): link the mechanism to earnings without a guaranteed universal result.
objective_titles: Analyse and discuss changes in earnings over time between occupations and between economic sectors

items.prompt: Explain the purchasing-power change when invented monthly pay rises from N$2,000 to N$2,200 and the price of the worker’s consumption bundle rises by 10%.
items.canonical_answer: Pay and the bundle price both rise by 10%. N$2,200 buys the same bundle as N$2,000 previously, so purchasing power is unchanged on this measure.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Analyse and discuss changes in earnings over time between occupations and between economic sectors

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between transfer earnings and economic rent within a factor reward.
items.canonical_answer: Transfer earnings are the minimum reward required to keep the factor in its present use. Economic rent is the excess of the actual reward over that minimum.
marking_guidance: Difference (1): minimum required reward. Contrast/test (1): excess above that minimum.
objective_titles: Explain economic rent and transfer earnings

items.prompt: Explain the split of an invented N$6,000 monthly reward when N$5,000 is stated to be the minimum required to keep the worker in the present use.
items.canonical_answer: Transfer earnings are N$5,000. Economic rent is N$6,000 minus N$5,000, giving N$1,000; the two parts sum to the actual reward.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition.
objective_titles: Explain economic rent and transfer earnings

items.prompt: Explain the confusion in calling a hypothetical support payment received without current work supplied in exchange “transfer earnings”.
items.canonical_answer: That is a transfer payment. Transfer earnings instead mean the minimum factor reward required to retain a resource in its present use; the shared word transfer does not make the concepts equivalent.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): payment without current production is mistaken for a factor’s required reward. Boundary/test (1): minimum needed to retain the factor distinguishes transfer earnings.
objective_titles: Explain economic rent and transfer earnings

items.prompt: Define transfer earnings (2). Identify two factors determining earnings (2). Explain one difference in invented monthly earnings where specialists are scarce, assistants are readily available and hours match (2). Identify the transfer earnings and economic rent within a N$7,000 reward when the minimum required to retain the worker is N$5,500 (2).
items.canonical_answer: Transfer earnings are the minimum reward required to keep a factor in its present use. Demand for labour and supply of suitable workers affect earnings. Scarcity makes specialists harder to recruit, supporting higher offers than for readily available assistants under the stated conditions. Transfer earnings are N$5,500 and economic rent N$1,500.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): minimum reward (1), retaining factor in present use (1). Separate points for factors (2): labour demand (1), suitable labour supply (1). Explanation (2): specialist scarcity (1), competitive offers can raise relative earnings (1). Identification (2): transfer earnings N$5,500 (1), rent N$1,500 (1). Marks allocation 8.
objective_titles: Explain economic rent and transfer earnings

items.prompt: Invented same-hours monthly data: technical workers earn N$5,000 in Year 1 and N$6,000 in Year 2; assistants earn N$4,000 then N$4,200. Technical output per hour rises 20%, orders increase and suitably trained applicants remain scarce. Assistant output per hour is unchanged and many applicants are available. Technical workers negotiate collectively; assistants have weak bargaining strength. In Year 2 the stated minimum needed to retain a technical worker is N$5,200. Describe three features: one labour-demand influence, one labour-supply influence and the transfer earnings/economic-rent split for the Year 2 technical reward (6). Explain a mechanism supporting the earnings difference between technical workers and assistants, including the role of alternatives in the technical reward split (7). Discuss whether productivity alone adequately explains the different earnings changes (7).
items.canonical_answer: Orders support technical labour demand; scarce trained applicants restrict suitable supply. Year 2 technical transfer earnings are N$5,200 and rent is N$800. Strong demand and restricted skill supply encourage higher technical offers than for readily available assistants. Alternatives determine the minimum needed to retain the technical worker, so N$5,200 is the required part and N$800 the excess. Technical pay rises 20% while assistants’ pay rises 5%. Productivity supports the technical rise, but scarcity, orders and bargaining also support it; the data cannot isolate their contributions. Productivity alone is an incomplete account.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): stronger technical labour demand (1), increased orders detail (1); restricted supply (1), scarce trained applicants detail (1); transfer earnings N$5,200 (1), rent N$800 (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): orders create worker demand (1), scarce skills constrain recruitment (1), competitive technical offers follow (1); assistants more readily replaceable (1); alternatives determine retention minimum (1), N$5,200 required (1), remaining N$800 rent (1). Both sides/judgement (7): technical pay rises 20% (1), productivity also rises 20% supporting account (1); assistants rise 5% without productivity gain (1), bargaining and scarcity offer additional explanations (1); separate effects not identified (1); conclude productivity alone incomplete (1), conditional on supplied evidence rather than assumed single cause (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

facts: Invented same-hours monthly data: technical workers earn N$5,000 in Year 1 and N$6,000 in Year 2; assistants earn N$4,000 then N$4,200. Technical output per hour rises 20%, orders increase and suitably trained applicants remain scarce. Assistant output per hour is unchanged and many applicants are available. Technical workers negotiate collectively; assistants have weak bargaining strength. In Year 2 the stated minimum needed to retain a technical worker is N$5,200.

objective_titles: Identify and analyse the factors determining earnings

items.prompt: Invented same-hours cases. Case 1: repair technicians’ usable output per hour rises 20%, customer orders rise, trained applicants remain scarce and bargaining is strong; their pay rises 15%, compared with 3% for general assistants whose productivity is unchanged. Case 2: routine service workers’ output per hour is unchanged, many applicants seek the work, bargaining is weak and pay rises 2%; another occupation with scarce relevant skills receives 12%. No price-level data are supplied. Evaluate the productivity explanation of relative earnings changes in Case 1 (7). Evaluate whether a substantial pay rise for routine service workers is well supported by the evidence in Case 2 (7). Present two conditional plans.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: greater technical productivity and orders support stronger labour demand and capacity to fund pay; unchanged assistant productivity supports the relative contrast. Scarcity and bargaining also matter, so the evidence supports productivity as part of the account rather than a measured sole cause. Case 2: unchanged productivity, readily available applicants and weak bargaining give limited support for a substantial routine-worker rise. The observed 2% shows some increase can occur, while the scarce-skill occupation faces different conditions. A larger future rise needs additional demand, supply or bargaining evidence; neither case establishes real-pay changes without prices.
marking_guidance: Case 1 allocation (7): argument for productivity contribution (1), link to funded demand (1); argument against sole-cause account from scarcity (1), bargaining (1); condition separate contributions unknown (1); judgement productivity contributes (1), insufficient alone (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument against large rise from unchanged productivity (1), plentiful applicants/weak bargaining (1); argument for some increase shown by 2% (1), changed demand could alter future outcome (1); condition additional evidence needed (1); judgement substantial rise weakly supported (1), link to differing scarce-skill conditions (1). Total marks 14.
